chapter: Handy, Bix and disputes over credit
title: Giving credit and the young Bix Beiderbecke
summary: He says others resent him, and tells how a teenage Bix came to him in New York, stayed and returned in 1923.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: Well, Sharky might because Sharky got up and Sharky lost his place in the jazz club by telling the people I was the one who brought this music around the world. Sharky was pulled off a program for the same thing. Now, Sharky was born about eight, nine years old when I was a musician playing music. Sharky wasn't playing music. Harry Shields wasn't playing music. Parenti wasn't playing music. George's Brunessons that they played. They weren't around. But they all got their mouth open big as an alligator trying to get some credit. They did not do them. And I didn't think it was fair. They said, I never give people credit. I have given people credit. I have given Armstrong credit. I have given Big Spider back his due credit. He tried to start a new style. And I'll show you where he got his style. Da-na-na-na-na-na-na-na. I'll reverse that. I can't think of it now what he uses in his thing. Because offhand you get mixed up. It'll come to me after. And many in the licks did. Big Spade. I showed him. He came to me as a school boy when he was 17 years of age. He ran away from home. These people ran a phonograph store. At that time there was only one jazz band. He liked it. Come to see what we looked like. And he come and asked the doorman, could he get in? They looked at him, he was two years old. He said, my daddy plays from the band. He didn't know me or I didn't know him. So he came on up there and he said, Mr. LaRocco, just like he know me. And I had to get him off the floor and I said, sit back here, son. I thought he was a boy from New Orleans. And I let him sit back there. That night I seen he didn't have no place to go. Well, I used to go out most every night and I had a room doing nothing. I told him, you got a place to sleep? He said, no. I brought him to my place and play my carnet all day. Play on the carnet. Asked me to show him different things, which I did. I kept him there a week. And the boys in the band turned and said, Nick, you're doing the wrong thing. You're harboring a minor. You're liable to get in trouble. You understand you better send that kid back home. So I got him, put him on the train. Paid my own money for him. And sent him back to Davenport where he lived. 1923, he comes again. This time he plays. He's playing pretty good corner. He sit in and I let him sit in the band. He played. He played all my numbers. The only numbers he styled himself on. He don't have a place to stand, huh? But he meets a buddy about his own age. I had, Lawrence had quit the band. And this fellow, Jimmy Lytell, had wended. And they formed the Memphis Five, which was a Brooklyn organization. And I had taken out and saw the Seaboy. The Seaboy was about Bix's age and then bummed together. But I had to feed him every day. There was a restaurant called Demi's Restaurant. He could go in there anytime he wanted and get food. And I paid the tab for him. He stayed there about three, four weeks. Then just by loaning the money, go back home. I have letters right here that you can see.
Now, I know you or I, we don't want to take credit away from Bix for what he had. Bix is a great man. Yes.
